titel: Taxes and practicalities in US trading
kurz: Trading gains are taxed per calendar year, short-term gains at the full income tax rate, nobody withholds the tax for you, and almost none of a private trader's expenses are deductible.

bloecke.md:
Every closed position is a taxable event. It makes no difference whether it belonged to a series that only pays off over two years or whether its gain was already earmarked for the next trade. The tax is calculated per calendar year, and US brokers do not withhold it. You pay it yourself, during the year through estimated tax payments.

This gives rise to three effects through which a strategy that works on paper can fail in the account. Short-term gains are taxed at the full income tax rate, the tax for a good year falls due even if the next year starts with losses, and the costs of running the trading operation are not deductible for most private traders. Together with spreads and slippage, these effects considerably raise the threshold above which trading pays off.

## Tax rate and holding period

For tax purposes, the decisive line is one year. Gains on stocks, ETFs and options held for one year or less are short-term capital gains and are taxed like wages at your [[Marginal tax rate|marginal tax rate]], which ranges from 10% to 37% in 2026. Gains on positions held for more than a year are long-term and are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)). Almost all gains of an active trader are short-term. Above a modified adjusted gross income of $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly), the net investment income tax of 3.8% is added, and most states tax capital gains as ordinary income as well.

The type of instrument determines the holding period rules, the timing of the tax and the form on which the result is reported. Of all the tax distinctions, these have the greatest financial consequences in trading.

bloecke.md:
Within a year, all capital gains and losses are netted against each other, first within the short-term and the long-term group, then across them (Schedule D). There are no separate pots for different instruments: a loss on options can offset a gain on stocks and vice versa. If a net loss remains, up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately) reduces other income such as wages (26 U.S.C. § 1211(b)). The rest is carried forward indefinitely and keeps its short- or long-term character (§ 1212(b)). Individuals cannot carry losses back to earlier years, with one exception for Section 1256 contracts.

The most important restriction for traders is the wash sale rule (26 U.S.C. § 1091). If you sell at a loss and buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed for now. It is added to the cost basis of the new shares, and their holding period includes that of the old ones. The rule also applies when the purchase is made in another of your accounts, by your spouse or in an IRA, where the loss is then lost for good. Brokers only report wash sales within the same account and for identical securities; everything else is your responsibility.

bloecke.titel: Loss after the turn of the year
bloecke.md:
An account closes December with a realized net short-term gain of $40,000. At a marginal tax rate of 24%, applied to the whole amount for simplicity, this means $9,600 of federal tax for that year. In January, the same strategy loses the same $40,000.

Economically, the trader is back at zero before tax. The tax for the previous year is nevertheless final, and it falls due only now: with the last estimated payment on January 15 or with the return by April 15. In the new year, the January loss can reduce other income by only $3,000, worth $720 at 24%; the remaining $37,000 is carried forward and only takes effect against future gains. In addition, the trading capital is permanently $9,600 smaller, and with it every future position.

bloecke.titel: Trading year with $50,000 of capital, from gross to net
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with 100 round turns a year at full account size, total costs of 0.10% per round turn and short-term gains taxed at a federal marginal rate of 24%, without NIIT and state income tax. A gross 16% becomes a net 4.6%.

bloecke.md:
Hardly any of the costs in this example are commissions, which are zero for stocks and ETFs at the large online brokers. They come from the spread, from slippage and, for options and futures, from per-contract fees. State income tax would reduce the result further, by up to 13.3% in California and not at all in states without an income tax such as Florida or Texas.

The calculation can also be reversed. It then shows how much a strategy has to earn gross for a modest net return to remain after costs and tax. The result depends almost entirely on the trading frequency. Costs grow linearly with the number of round turns, whereas the tax only covers what is left after costs.

bloecke.titel: Gross return required for a net 4%
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with total costs of 0.10% per round turn (commission and fees, half the spread per side, slippage) on the full account volume, followed by 24% federal tax on the short-term result after costs, without NIIT and state income tax.

bloecke.md:
With 250 round turns, the strategy has to earn more than 30% a year for 4% to remain. Mistakes, slippage outliers and losing streaks are not yet included. Tax planning does not change this. The most important lever is the trading frequency; the tax acts only as a factor on the result after costs. Holding positions for more than a year would lower the rate to 15% for most people, but that is investing, not trading.

## Section 1256 contracts

Regulated futures and options on broad-based indices, such as options on the S&P 500 index itself, follow special rules (26 U.S.C. § 1256). Open positions are treated as sold at fair market value on December 31, and every gain or loss counts as 60% long-term and 40% short-term, regardless of the holding period. In the 24% bracket with a 15% long-term rate, a gain of $10,000 costs $1,860 in federal tax instead of $2,400 for a short-term stock gain; at the top rates, the blended rate is 26.8% instead of 37%. Options on ETFs such as SPY are not Section 1256 contracts, even though they track the same index. A net loss on Section 1256 contracts can be carried back three years against Section 1256 gains of those years (§ 1212(c)).

bloecke.md:
## Liquidity and timing of the tax

US brokers do not withhold tax on capital gains. They deduct 24% backup withholding only if you have not provided a correct taxpayer identification number on Form W-9. The tax on trading gains is therefore due through quarterly estimated payments on Form 1040-ES, on April 15, June 15 and September 15 of the year and on January 15 of the following year, moved to the next business day where necessary. If you pay too little, a penalty is charged that works like interest on the shortfall.

There is no penalty if your payments and withholding reach at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax; if last year's adjusted gross income was above $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately), the second figure is 110% (IRS Publication 505). For traders whose income fluctuates, the prior-year rule is the practical safe harbor. If the gains are concentrated late in the year, the annualized income installment method on Form 2210 can reduce or avoid the penalty for the earlier quarters. Employees can also raise the withholding from their paychecks, which counts as paid evenly over the year.

bloecke.titel: Worked example of the safe harbor
bloecke.md:
A single trader had a total federal tax of $12,000 last year, with adjusted gross income below $150,000. This year, trading gains raise the tax to $30,000.

- The safe harbor is 100% of last year's tax, so four estimated payments of $3,000 are enough to avoid a penalty.
- The remaining $18,000 is due with the tax return by April 15 of the following year.
- If last year's adjusted gross income had been above $150,000, the safe harbor would be 110%, that is $13,200 or four payments of $3,300.

The safe harbor protects against the penalty, not against the tax. The $18,000 must be available in April, even if the account has lost money in the meantime. Active traders should therefore set aside part of every realized gain in a separate cash account.

## Option writer's premiums

An [[Option writer's premium|option writer's premium]] is not taxed when it is received. The position stays open for tax purposes until it ends (IRS Publication 550). If the option expires, the premium becomes a short-term capital gain in the year of expiration. If you buy the option back, the difference between the premium received and the price paid is a short-term gain or loss in the year of closing (26 U.S.C. § 1234(b)). If a written call is exercised, the premium is added to the sale proceeds of the stock; if a written put is exercised, it reduces the cost basis of the stock you buy. A premium collected in December and bought back in January is therefore taxed only in the year in which the economic result is known.

There are two exceptions. Written options on broad-based indices are Section 1256 contracts and are marked to market on December 31 like futures. In addition, positions that offset each other's risk, such as a covered call written deep in the money or a hedged pair of positions, can form a straddle. Losses on one leg are then deferred as long as the offsetting position has an unrealized gain (26 U.S.C. § 1092).

## Records and foreign brokers

US brokers report every sale on Form 1099-B, including the cost basis for covered securities: stocks bought since 2011, most fund shares since 2012, options and most bonds since 2014. They must furnish the form by February 15; corrected forms often follow later. From the 1099-B, the trades go onto Form 8949 and Schedule D, and Section 1256 contracts onto Form 6781. If the cost basis is missing, for example for positions transferred from a foreign broker or bought before the reporting rules applied, you have to supply it yourself. If you cannot prove it, you risk being taxed on the full proceeds.

Foreign brokers do not issue a 1099-B. The calculation, the conversion of foreign currency amounts into dollars and the reporting are then your own responsibility. Foreign accounts must also be reported to the Treasury on the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) if their combined value exceeded $10,000 at any time during the year, and above higher thresholds on Form 8938 with the tax return. Gains and losses on foreign currency balances generally count as ordinary income under 26 U.S.C. § 988. A trading journal, which should be kept anyway, in practice also covers these records.

bloecke.titel: Realized gains and losses over the full year and in December
bloecke.unter: Odean (1998), around 10,000 US brokerage accounts, 1987-1993. PGR and PLR measure the proportion of realized gain and loss positions respectively, relative to the gain and loss positions that could have been realized.

bloecke.md: In December the ratio reverses, that is, at the time when selling at a loss brings a tax advantage. This shows that investors are able to realize losses. In the other eleven months, they sell losing positions much less often than winning positions. For traders, a year-end review is therefore justified. At the same time, it is the point at which tax reasons begin to determine trading decisions. A position that should be held under your own rules should not be sold solely to harvest a loss, and if you want to keep the exposure, the wash sale rule only lets you buy it back after 30 days.

1. Add up realized short-term and long-term gains and losses across all your accounts, including those at different brokers.
2. Before selling at a loss, check whether you bought the same security in the previous 30 days in any account, including IRAs, and do not buy it back in the 30 days after the sale.
3. Check whether your estimated payments and withholding reach the safe harbor, and plan the cash for the payment due on January 15.
4. For foreign brokers, check whether all annual statements are available and the amounts have been converted into dollars.

Closing positions purely for tax reasons does not belong on this list.

bloecke.titel: Investor or trader in the eyes of the IRS
bloecke.md:
Frequent trading alone does not make you a trader for tax purposes. According to the IRS and the case law of the Tax Court, trader tax status requires that you seek to profit from daily market movements rather than from dividends, interest or long-term appreciation, and that your trading is substantial, regular and continuous (IRS Topic No. 429). There is no fixed number of trades; courts have denied the status to taxpayers with many trades a year whose holding periods were long or whose trading was not continuous.

This classification has advantages and disadvantages. With trader tax status, you can deduct trading expenses such as data feeds, software and a home office on Schedule C; the gains remain capital gains and are not subject to self-employment tax. With an additional mark-to-market election under 26 U.S.C. § 475(f), all positions are treated as sold at the end of the year, gains and losses become ordinary, and the wash sale rule and the $3,000 limit no longer apply, but long-term rates are lost for these positions. The election must be made by the original due date of the tax return for the year before the year in which it is to apply, and it remains in force for later years until it is revoked.

mitnehmen: Gains on positions held for a year or less are taxed at the marginal tax rate of up to 37%, and US brokers do not withhold the tax; it is due through estimated payments.
All capital gains and losses of a year are netted without separate pots; a net loss reduces other income by up to $3,000 and is otherwise carried forward indefinitely, but not back.
The wash sale rule disallows a loss if the same security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale, across all your accounts including IRAs.
Section 1256 contracts such as regulated futures and broad-based index options are taxed 60/40 and marked to market at year-end; options on ETFs are not.
To make 4% after costs and 24% federal tax, a gross return of just over 15% is needed with 100 round turns a year, and more than 30% with 250 round turns.

begriffe.text: Sale of a security at a loss combined with a purchase of the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale (26 U.S.C. § 1091). The loss is disallowed for now and added to the cost basis of the new position; if the purchase is made in an IRA, the loss is lost.

Regulated futures contract, foreign currency contract, nonequity option such as a broad-based index option, or dealer equity option. It is marked to market on December 31, taxed 60% long-term and 40% short-term and reported on Form 6781.

Quarterly advance payments on income without withholding, such as trading gains (Form 1040-ES). A penalty applies if the payments fall short of the safe harbor of 90% of this year's tax or 100% (110% at higher incomes) of last year's tax.

Classification of securities trading as a business, based on substantial, regular and continuous trading aimed at short-term price movements. It allows trading expenses to be deducted on Schedule C; together with a Section 475(f) election, gains and losses become ordinary.

Closing an open derivatives position by means of the corresponding offsetting transaction; for the option writer, this means buying back the written option. For tax purposes, the gain or loss is realized at this point.
